title: Tools & MCP

techniques.name: Function Calling Basics
techniques.q: How does a model actually use a tool?
techniques.what: Each tool is a name, a description and a JSON Schema for its inputs. The model does not run anything: it returns a structured call, your code validates and runs it, and you send the result back under the same call id. The loop repeats until the model answers in text. tool_choice sets whether the model may, must or must not call a tool.
use: Any agent that must read live data or act: balances, orders, tickets
Turning free text into validated, typed arguments for an API
Replacing guesses with lookups, such as a UTR status check
metrics: request with tools → tool_use → run it → tool_result → repeat until end_turn
auto (default with tools), any, tool (force one), none
each result carries the tool_use_id (OpenAI: call_id) of its call
strict: true constrains sampling so inputs always match the schema
a failed call goes back as a tool_result with is_error: true, never dropped
OpenAI suggests fewer than 20 functions available at the start of a turn
steps: Write each tool as a name, a 3–4 sentence description and an input schema
Send tools with tool_choice auto; force a tool only when the step truly requires it
Validate the arguments, run the tool, and return every result under its own call id
Cap the loop with a step limit and return errors with is_error so the model can recover
pitfalls: Forcing a tool on every turn wastes calls and can stop the model from answering
Mismatched or reused call ids break the conversation
Some current models reject tool_choice any and tool with a 400 error, as does manual extended thinking
techniques.remember: The model asks; your code runs. Match every result to its call id.
techniques.cap: Illustrative numbers. One lookup costs one extra model turn: 2 turns, 1 call.

techniques.name: Tool Interface Design
techniques.q: Will the model use this tool well?
techniques.what: A tool’s name, description, parameters, results and errors are a prompt the model reads every turn. Good design consolidates several API calls into one task-shaped tool, names parameters without ambiguity, returns only high-signal fields, and turns errors into instructions the model can act on. Measure it on a task set, like any prompt.
use: Agents with many overlapping tools that pick the wrong one
Tools that return large raw records or opaque error codes
Wrapping an existing API for use by agents
metrics: by far the most important factor; 3–4 sentences or more
one schedule_event instead of list_users + list_events + create_event
unambiguous names (user_id, not user), enums, defaults
semantic fields, pagination and a concise response_format
say what was wrong and how to fix it
load definitions on demand with tool search past roughly 30–50 tools
steps: Start from real tasks and merge chains of thin endpoints into task-shaped tools
Write descriptions: what it does, when to use it, when not to, and caveats
Trim results to the fields the next step needs; add pagination and a concise mode
Return actionable errors, then evaluate on a task set and read the wrong-choice transcripts
pitfalls: Near-duplicate tools (search_txn, find_transaction) split the model’s choices
Raw payloads fill the context and bury the field that matters
Opaque codes such as E422 leave the model retrying blind
techniques.remember: Design tools for the model that reads them, not for the API behind them.
techniques.cap: Illustrative results on a 10-task set. Token counts echo Anthropic’s example of concise responses.

cmp.needs: Low to medium: task set, rewrites

techniques.name: Parallel and Sequential Tool Calls
techniques.q: Which calls can go out together?
techniques.what: A model can emit several independent calls in one turn. Your code can run them concurrently, so the wait becomes the slowest call instead of the sum. A call that needs another call’s output must wait for it. All results go back together, and a failure in the batch must not drop its siblings.
use: Several independent lookups per request: KYC checks, fare searches
Fan-out reads across services before one decision
Latency-sensitive assistants where every second counts
metrics: wall-clock falls from the sum to the critical path
all tool_result blocks in one user message, before any text
each failed or skipped call still gets a result with is_error
a call that needs another’s output runs after it
BFCL scores simple, multiple, parallel and parallel-multiple calls
steps: Collect every tool_use block in the response
Classify each call: independent read, dependent, or side-effecting
Run independent calls together with per-call timeouts; run dependent calls in order
Return one message with all results, errors marked, then measure the critical path
pitfalls: Running a dependent call in the same batch as its input: it reads an id that does not exist yet
Letting one exception cancel the batch so no results go back
Splitting results across messages, which discourages parallel calls later
techniques.remember: Sum becomes max, but only for calls that do not depend on each other.
techniques.cap: Illustrative KYC latencies. The four lookups run together; open_account waits for all four.

techniques.name: Retries, Timeouts and Idempotency
techniques.q: Is it safe to try that again?
techniques.what: Tool calls time out, drop connections and return 5xx errors. Reads can be retried freely. A write that moves money or sends a message needs an idempotency key, created once per logical action, so a retry returns the first result instead of repeating the action. Every call gets a timeout, and retries use capped exponential backoff with jitter. This technique makes one call safe to repeat; the AgentOps module covers protecting the whole system when a dependency keeps failing.
use: Tools that pay, refund, debit, book or send messages
Gateways and partner APIs that time out under load
Durable workflows that replay steps after a crash
metrics: timeouts, 429 and 5xx; never a 4xx that will fail again
one per logical action, reused on every retry
store the first response per key; replay it; reject a changed payload
idempotentHint defaults to false, destructiveHint to true
steps: Label every tool as a read, an idempotent write or a non-idempotent write
Put a timeout on every call and retry only timeouts, 429 and 5xx
Back off exponentially with full jitter and a cap on attempts
Create the key once per action; have the server store and replay results by key
pitfalls: A fresh key on every attempt looks safe but repeats the action
Retrying in lockstep turns a brief outage into a retry storm
A lost response after success is the dangerous case: the action happened, the client does not know
techniques.remember: One action, one key, every retry.
techniques.cap: Illustrative UPI refund. The retry reuses key 7f3c, so the gateway replays the stored result.

cmp.needs: Medium: key store on the server

techniques.name: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
techniques.q: How do I plug tools into any agent?
techniques.what: An open JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol for connecting AI applications to tools and data. A host (the AI app) runs one client per server; servers offer tools (model-controlled), resources (context data) and prompts (user-chosen templates). Revision 2026-07-28 made the core stateless: no initialize handshake or session header, and every request carries its protocol version and capabilities in _meta.
use: One set of tools shared by several assistants, IDEs and agents
Exposing internal systems to third-party AI apps under OAuth
Replacing per-framework tool adapters with one server
metrics: host → one client per server → server
server/discover, subscriptions/listen, input_required retries, ttlMs caching
HTTP only: OAuth 2.1, protected resource metadata, audience-checked tokens
donated to the Agentic AI Foundation (Linux Foundation), December 2025
steps: Build a server with an SDK and give each tool a schema, annotations and an output schema
Add resources for context data and prompts for user-chosen templates
Serve over stdio locally or Streamable HTTP remotely
Protect HTTP with OAuth: 401 with resource metadata, scopes, audience checks, no token passthrough
pitfalls: Tool descriptions from untrusted servers are an injection surface (tool poisoning)
Annotations such as readOnlyHint are hints; trust them only from trusted servers
Forwarding the client’s token to downstream APIs breaks the audience boundary
techniques.remember: Write the server once; every MCP host can use it.
techniques.cap: One client per server connection. Tools are called by the model; resources and prompts are chosen by the app or user.

techniques.name: Agent-to-Agent Protocols (A2A)
techniques.q: How does my agent hand work to another agent?
techniques.what: A2A lets one agent delegate a task to an opaque remote agent, usually one run by another organisation. The client discovers the remote agent through its Agent Card, sends messages, and tracks a Task through states such as working, input required and completed, by polling, streaming or push notifications, then collects the artifacts it returns. MCP connects an agent to tools; A2A connects agents as peers.
use: Handing a whole goal to a partner’s agent: rebooking, claims, estimates
Long-running work with questions back to the requester
Agents built on different frameworks or by different companies
metrics: /.well-known/agent-card.json: identity, skills, capabilities, security schemes, signatures
WORKING, INPUT_REQUIRED, AUTH_REQUIRED, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELED, REJECTED
poll with GetTask, stream updates, or push notifications
Linux Foundation project since June 2025; joined the Agentic AI Foundation in August 2026
steps: Decide whether you need a tool (one function) or an agent (a goal with judgment)
Publish an Agent Card with skills, capabilities and security schemes, and sign it
Discover and verify the remote card, then send a message and receive a Task
Handle INPUT_REQUIRED, stream or push updates, and collect artifacts; map failures to your retry policy
pitfalls: Treating INPUT_REQUIRED as a failure: it is an interrupted state waiting for your answer
Delegating a deterministic lookup that should be an API or MCP tool
Trusting an unsigned or unverified card from an unknown domain
techniques.remember: Tools get calls. Agents get tasks.
techniques.cap: Illustrative flight rebooking. The task pauses once for a question, then completes with an artifact.

cmp.best: Delegating what a tool could do

techniques.name: Tool Search and Large Tool Sets
techniques.q: How does the agent find the right tool among hundreds?
techniques.what: Loading every tool definition into every prompt stops working past a few dozen tools: the definitions eat the context and similar tools blur together. Instead, keep a handful of frequently used tools loaded, mark the rest as deferred, and give the model a search tool. When it needs a capability it searches, the matching definitions are loaded, and it calls the one it needs. Anthropic’s API offers regex and BM25 tool search, and you can plug in your own, such as embedding search.
use: Agents connected to several MCP servers with hundreds of tools
Tool definitions that take more than about 10,000 tokens a turn
A tool library that grows every month
metrics: sent with every request but hidden from the model until a search finds them (defer_loading)
the 3–5 most used tools stay visible, so common tasks skip the search
regex or BM25 over names and descriptions, or your own embedding search
a few tool references per search, expanded into full definitions
they are the search index: clear names and the words users actually say
right-tool rate, searches that find nothing, tokens per turn and the extra step
steps: Measure definition tokens per turn and the right-tool rate on a task set
Keep the most-used tools loaded and defer the rest
Add a search tool, and rewrite names and descriptions so the right words find each tool
Measure again, and log every search that found nothing useful
pitfalls: A tool with a vague name and description is never found, so it is never used
Deferring everything adds a search step to even the most common tasks
Near-duplicate tools from different servers still confuse the model once found
techniques.remember: Load a few, search for the rest. Descriptions are the index.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: a back-office agent at Nivesh Setu, a fictional wealth platform, with 240 tools across 6 MCP servers.

cmp.scope: Which tools the model sees each turn
cmp.needs: Medium: a search tool and good descriptions

techniques.name: Tool Authentication and Scoped Permissions
techniques.q: Whose credentials does each tool call carry, and for what?
techniques.what: Each tool call the agent makes reaches a real API with some credential. Instead of one shared service key that can touch every customer, the user signs in and consents through OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, and the agent receives a delegated token for that user only. Each tool gets the narrowest scope it needs, access tokens live minutes and are renewed silently, and tokens sit in a vault that the tool layer reads, never in the prompt. Disconnecting revokes them, and every call is logged under the user. The MCP technique covers what a server must check; action policies decide whether a call is allowed; this is about the credentials the call carries.
use: Agents that act on a customer’s own accounts: portfolios, bank data, email, calendars
Connecting to remote MCP servers or SaaS APIs on behalf of many users
Anywhere an auditor asks which user a tool call acted for
metrics: issued to the agent for one user after that user consents; calls act as that user
authorization code flow with an S256 code challenge, so a stolen code cannot be redeemed
one per tool and verb, such as portfolio:read or redeem:write; writes asked for when needed
access tokens last minutes to an hour; rotating refresh tokens renew them silently
encrypted, per user, outside the prompt; the tool layer attaches the token to the call
disconnecting revokes the refresh token; each call is logged with user, tool and scope
steps: List each tool with the API it calls and the narrowest scope it needs
Get a per-user token with OAuth 2.1 + PKCE, asking for read scopes first and writes only when needed
Keep tokens in a vault; the tool layer attaches them, the model only sees results
Use short-lived access tokens with rotating refresh, revoke on disconnect, and log every call under the user
pitfalls: One shared service key lets any prompt injection reach every customer’s account
A token pasted into the prompt can be echoed out by the model or land in traces and logs
Asking for every scope at sign-up means a read-only question carries redeem rights
techniques.remember: Act as the user, only for this tool, only for a few minutes. Keep the key out of the prompt.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Dhan Disha, a fictional wealth app, with 50,000 users who connected their accounts to its assistant.

cmp.needs: Medium: an authorization server, a vault, refresh handling
cmp.best: Shared keys and scopes granted once and forgotten

techniques.name: Agent Skills
techniques.q: How do I give an agent many procedures without flooding its context?
techniques.what: A skill is a folder with instructions, scripts and reference files for one kind of task. Only each skill’s name and short description sit in the agent’s context; the full instructions load when a task matches, and bundled scripts run as code rather than being re-derived by the model. This progressive disclosure lets one agent carry dozens of procedures cheaply. Skills are code: review them, version them, and never install one you have not read.
use: Operations agents with many written procedures
Company-specific formats, checklists and templates
Deterministic steps worth a script, such as date calculations or file checks
metrics: specific enough that the agent picks the right one
body and files load only when relevant
forms, policies and examples read on demand
skills change behaviour like code does
third-party skills can carry harmful instructions
steps: Write one skill per procedure: a folder with SKILL.md, scripts and references
Make the description say what it does and when to use it
Move deterministic steps into scripts the skill runs
Review, version and test skills; read any third-party skill before installing
pitfalls: Vague descriptions, so the wrong skill loads
Pasting every procedure into the system prompt instead
Installing a downloaded skill without reading it
techniques.remember: Describe it well, load it late, script the exact parts.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Paisapath, a fictional fintech, runs 30 operations procedures through one agent.

fcall
Get the loop right: clear schemas, tool_choice auto, strict inputs, and results matched to call ids.
It picks the wrong tool, fills arguments badly or drowns in output
tooldesign
Merge overlapping tools, write full descriptions, trim results and make errors actionable.
Independent lookups run one after another
parallel
Run independent calls in one turn concurrently and return all results together.
A retry could charge, refund or email twice
idempotency
Give each action one idempotency key, reuse it on every retry, and back off with jitter.
One set of tools should serve many apps and agents
mcp
Expose them once as an MCP server; any MCP host can discover and call them.
A whole task must go to another organisation’s agent
a2a
Delegate it over A2A: discover the Agent Card, send a task, track its states and collect artifacts.
The agent has hundreds of tools and keeps picking the wrong one
toolsearch
Keep a few common tools loaded, defer the rest behind a search tool, and write descriptions that match how people ask.
The agent’s tools use one shared API key, or a token sits in the prompt
toolauth
Give each user a delegated OAuth token with one scope per tool, keep it short-lived in a vault the model never sees, and log every call under the user.
The agent needs dozens of procedures and the prompt is huge
skills
Package each procedure as a skill: short description up front, instructions and scripts loaded only when needed.

import json, anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

TOOLS = [{
    "name": "get_transaction_status",                                      #@1
    "description": ("Look up a UPI payment by its 12-digit UTR number. "    #@1
                    "Use it whenever the user asks if a payment went through. "   #@1
                    "Never guess a status; ask for the UTR if it is missing. "    #@1
                    "Returns status, amount in INR and last update time."),     #@1
    "input_schema": {"type": "object",                                     #@1
                     "properties": {"utr": {"type": "string"}},            #@1
                     "required": ["utr"], "additionalProperties": False},  #@1,4
    "strict": True,                          # inputs always match the schema  #@4
}]
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Did UTR 412345678901 go through?"}]

for turn in range(6):                        # step cap                     #@6
    resp = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=1024,   #@2
                                  tools=TOOLS, tool_choice={"type": "auto"},   #@2
                                  messages=messages)                          #@2
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":                                        #@3,6
        break                                # the model answered in text      #@3,6
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})          #@3
    results = []
    for block in (b for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"):          #@3
        try:
            out = run_tool(block.name, block.input)   # validate, then run    #@4
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,   #@5
                            "content": json.dumps(out)})                      #@5
        except Exception as e:                                                #@5
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,   #@5
                            "content": f"Lookup failed: {e}", "is_error": True})   #@5
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})                    #@5,6
steps: Define the tool
A name, a description of three or four sentences that says when to use it and when not, and a JSON Schema for the one argument, the UTR.
Send tools and tool_choice
The request carries the tool list and tool_choice auto, so the model may answer directly or call a tool. Forcing a call is only for steps that must produce one.
Detect a tool call
The response stops with stop_reason tool_use and contains a tool_use block: an id (toolu_01), the tool name and the arguments. The model has run nothing.
Validate and run
Your code checks the arguments against the schema and runs the lookup. With strict mode the arguments always match the schema, so this check rarely fails.
Return the result under the same id
Each tool_result carries the tool_use_id of the call it answers. A failure goes back too, with is_error true, so the model can recover instead of guessing.
Loop with a step cap
The loop sends the history back until the model answers in text. Here that is turn 2: one call, two model turns. The cap of 6 stops a runaway loop.

from datetime import date
from typing import Annotated, Literal
from fastmcp import FastMCP
from fastmcp.exceptions import ToolError

mcp = FastMCP("opd-scheduling")

@mcp.tool                                                    # one task, one tool   #@1
def find_free_slot(                                                                  #@1
    department: Literal["cardiology", "orthopaedics", "general_medicine"],           #@3
    on_date: Annotated[date, "Clinic date, ISO 8601, e.g. 2026-10-03"],              #@3
    response_format: Literal["concise", "detailed"] = "concise",                     #@3,4
) -> list[dict]:
    """Find doctors with free OPD slots in one department on one date.               #@2
    Use it before book_opd_slot: it already checks rosters, leave and bookings.      #@1,2
    Do not use it for a patient's existing appointments.                             #@2
    Returns at most 10 doctors; 'concise' gives id, name and free times only."""     #@2,4
    if on_date < date.today():                                                       #@5
        raise ToolError(f"on_date must be today or later; you sent {on_date}. "     #@5
                        "Check the year and call again.")                            #@5
    rows = ehr.free_slots(department, on_date)[:10]                                  #@1,4
    if response_format == "concise":                                                 #@4
        return [{"doctor_id": r.id, "name": r.name, "free": r.times} for r in rows]  #@4
    return [r.model_dump() for r in rows]                                            #@4

# Evaluate on real requests; read every transcript with a wrong choice              #@6
for case in load_cases("opd_requests.jsonl"):                                       #@6
    run = agent.run(case.prompt)                                                     #@6
    report(case.expected_tool, run.tool_calls, run.retries)                          #@6
steps: Start from the task
Booking needs one question answered: who is free, and when? One find_free_slot tool replaces four thin endpoints the model had to chain in the right order.
Write the description
Say what it does, when to use it, when not to, and what it returns. Anthropic calls the description by far the most important factor in tool performance.
Make parameters unambiguous
An enum for the department, a typed date with an example, and a default for response_format. The model cannot invent a department that does not exist.
Return only what the next step needs
The concise mode returns ids, names and free times, about 380 tokens instead of a 4,100-token roster record, and never more than 10 rows.
Turn errors into instructions
A past date gets a message that names the problem, the value sent and the fix. The model corrects the year in one retry instead of guessing.
Evaluate on a task set
Run real requests, score which tool was chosen and with which arguments, and read the wrong-choice transcripts. Tool design is prompt design, so measure it.

import asyncio, json, time

READS = {"pan_verify", "ckyc_search", "aadhaar_otp_status", "bureau_pull"}   #@2

async def run_one(block, timeout=3.0):                                       #@3
    try:
        out = await asyncio.wait_for(TOOLS[block.name](**block.input), timeout)   #@3
        return {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,              #@3
                "content": json.dumps(out)}                                  #@3
    except Exception as e:                        # never drop a result      #@5
        return {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,              #@5
                "content": f"Error: {e!r}", "is_error": True}                #@5

async def run_turn(resp):
    calls = [b for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]                #@1
    reads = [c for c in calls if c.name in READS]                            #@2
    rest = [c for c in calls if c.name not in READS]  # writes, dependents  #@2,4
    t0 = time.perf_counter()                                                 #@6
    results = list(await asyncio.gather(*(run_one(c) for c in reads)))      #@3
    failed = any(r.get("is_error") for r in results)
    for c in rest:                                # in order, after the join  #@4
        if failed:                                                           #@5
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": c.id,      #@5
                            "content": "Not executed: a lookup failed.",     #@5
                            "is_error": True})                               #@5
        else:
            results.append(await run_one(c))                                 #@4
    log.info("wall %.2fs", time.perf_counter() - t0)  # max(reads) + rest   #@6
    return {"role": "user", "content": results}   # all results, one message  #@5
steps: Collect every call
One response can contain several tool_use blocks. Here the model asks for four KYC lookups at once: PAN, CKYC, Aadhaar OTP status and the credit bureau.
Classify each call
The four lookups only read and do not need each other’s output, so they can run together. Writes and calls that need another call’s result go to a second group.
Run the reads together
asyncio.gather starts all four at once, each with its own timeout. The wait becomes the slowest lookup, 1,200 ms, not the 3,400 ms sum.
Run dependent calls after the join
open_account needs all four results, so it runs only after the join: 1,200 + 400 = 1,600 ms. In practice it often arrives in the model’s next turn.
Return every result in one message
A failed call returns is_error true, and a call skipped because of it says so. All results go back in one user message, one per tool_use_id.
Measure the critical path
Wall-clock time is the longest chain of dependent calls: bureau (1,200 ms), then open_account (400 ms). Adding more independent lookups barely changes it.

import httpx
from tenacity import retry, retry_if_exception, stop_after_attempt, wait_random_exponential

KIND = {"get_refund_status": "read",                                   #@1
        "set_mandate_limit": "idempotent_write",                       #@1
        "create_refund": "non_idempotent_write"}   # needs a key       #@1

def retryable(e: BaseException) -> bool:                               #@3
    if isinstance(e, httpx.TransportError):        # timeouts, resets  #@3
        return True                                                    #@3
    return isinstance(e, httpx.HTTPStatusError) and (                  #@3
        e.response.status_code == 429 or e.response.status_code >= 500)   #@3

@retry(retry=retry_if_exception(retryable),                            #@3
       wait=wait_random_exponential(multiplier=0.5, max=8),  # full jitter  #@4
       stop=stop_after_attempt(4), reraise=True)                       #@4
def post(path: str, body: dict, key: str) -> dict:
    r = http.post(path, json=body, timeout=10.0,                       #@2
                  headers={"Idempotency-Key": key})                     #@5
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()

def create_refund(dispute_id: str, amount_paise: int) -> dict:
    key = keys.get_or_create(f"refund/{dispute_id}")  # once per action  #@5
    return post("/v1/refunds", {"dispute": dispute_id, "amount": amount_paise}, key)   #@5

# Server side: the first request with a key runs; repeats get the stored response  #@6
def handle_refund(key: str, body: dict):                               #@6
    if not redis.set(f"idem:{key}", "running", nx=True, ex=86_400):    #@6
        return replay(key, body)   # stored result; 409 if running, 422 if body differs  #@6
    resp = do_refund(body); store(key, body, resp)                     #@6
    return resp                                                        #@6
steps: Classify the tools
Reads are always safe to retry. An idempotent write, such as setting a limit to ₹50,000, is safe too. A refund is a non-idempotent write: running it twice pays twice.
Give every call a timeout
The refund call waits at most 10 s. Without a timeout, a hung connection holds the agent’s turn for ever.
Retry only what can succeed
Timeouts, dropped connections, 429 and 5xx are worth another try. A 400 or 422 will fail the same way again, so it goes back to the model instead.
Back off with full jitter
Each retry waits a random time between zero and min(8 s, 0.5 s × 2^attempt), with at most 4 attempts, so clients that failed together do not retry together.
Create the key once per action
The key is derived from the dispute and stored, so every retry, and even a resumed agent, sends the same key for the same refund.
Store and replay on the server
The first request with a key runs and its response is stored for 24 hours. A repeat gets the stored response; a repeat with a different body gets 422.

from pydantic import BaseModel
from fastmcp import FastMCP
from fastmcp.server.auth.providers.jwt import JWTVerifier
from mcp.types import ToolAnnotations

# The host (an AI app or IDE) runs one MCP client per server. This file is a server.   #@1
auth = JWTVerifier(                                  # HTTP only; stdio uses env credentials   #@5
    jwks_uri="https://login.example-rta.in/.well-known/jwks.json",                   #@5
    issuer="https://login.example-rta.in",                                           #@5
    audience="https://mcp.example-rta.in/mcp",       # tokens issued for THIS server  #@5
)
mcp = FastMCP("folio-lookup", auth=auth)                                              #@1,5

class FolioSummary(BaseModel):                       # becomes the outputSchema       #@2
    folio: str; schemes: list[str]; units: float; nav_date: str                      #@2

@mcp.tool(annotations=ToolAnnotations(readOnlyHint=True, openWorldHint=False))        #@2
def get_folio_summary(folio: str) -> FolioSummary:                                    #@2
    """Schemes, units and latest NAV date for one mutual-fund folio. Read-only."""   #@2
    return registry.summary(folio)                                                    #@2

@mcp.resource("folio://schemes/{code}")              # context the app can read   #@3
def factsheet(code: str) -> str:                                                      #@3
    return factsheets[code]                                                           #@3

@mcp.prompt                                          # a template the user picks  #@3
def explain_statement(folio: str) -> str:                                             #@3
    return f"Explain the latest statement for folio {folio} in plain language."      #@3

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="http", host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)   # "stdio" when local      #@4
# Test: npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector, then tools/list and tools/call          #@6
steps: Host, client, server
The host is the AI application. It runs one MCP client per server it connects to, and each server exposes capabilities over JSON-RPC 2.0.
A tool with a schema and annotations
Type hints become the input schema and the return type becomes the output schema. Annotations such as readOnlyHint describe behaviour, but are only hints.
Resources and prompts
A resource is context data the application reads; a prompt is a template the user chooses. Tools are called by the model; the other two are not.
Pick a transport
stdio when the host starts the server as a local process; Streamable HTTP, a POST to one endpoint, when the server is remote and shared.
Protect the HTTP endpoint
A request without a token gets 401 pointing to the protected resource metadata. Tokens must be issued for this server (audience check), carry the right scopes, and are never passed through.
Test, then connect a host
MCP Inspector lists the tools and calls them by hand. Then add the server to a host; any MCP-compatible app can use it without new adapter code.

import time, uuid, httpx

# A tool is one function with a schema. An agent takes a goal and uses judgment.   #@1
# Our claims agent delegates estimate negotiation to the garage chain's agent.     #@1
MY_CARD = {"name": "Claims agent", "version": "1.0.0",                         #@2
           "supportedInterfaces": [{"url": "https://agents.example-ins.in/a2a",  #@2
                                    "protocolBinding": "JSONRPC"}],            #@2
           "capabilities": {"streaming": True, "pushNotifications": False},    #@2
           "skills": [{"id": "claim_status", "name": "Claim status",           #@2
                       "description": "Status of a motor claim"}]}   # signed at publish   #@2

BASE = "https://agents.example-garage.in"
card = httpx.get(f"{BASE}/.well-known/agent-card.json").json()                  #@3
verify_card_signature(card, trusted_keys)          # reject unsigned cards     #@3
assert any(s["id"] == "negotiate_estimate" for s in card["skills"])            #@3

task = rpc("SendMessage", msg("Agree a repair estimate for CLM-88412 within ₹62,000."))["task"]   #@4
TERMINAL = {"TASK_STATE_COMPLETED", "TASK_STATE_FAILED",                       #@4,6
            "TASK_STATE_CANCELED", "TASK_STATE_REJECTED"}                      #@4,6
for event in stream(task["id"]):                   # SubscribeToTask: no polling   #@5
    task = event.get("task", task) if "task" in event else apply(task, event)  #@5
    state = task["status"]["state"]                                            #@5
    if state == "TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED":       # interrupted, not failed    #@5
        answer = ask_claims_handler(task["status"]["message"])                 #@5
        rpc("SendMessage", msg(answer, taskId=task["id"], contextId=task["contextId"]))   #@5
    elif state in TERMINAL:                                                    #@6
        break                                                                  #@6
if state != "TASK_STATE_COMPLETED":
    raise DelegationFailed(state)                  # your retry policy decides   #@6
estimate = task["artifacts"][0]["parts"]           # the approved estimate      #@6
steps: Tool or agent?
A status lookup is one function: offer a tool or an API. Negotiating an estimate needs judgment, questions back and time, so it is delegated to an agent.
Publish your Agent Card
The card names the agent, where to reach it, what it can do (streaming, push), its skills and security schemes. Version 1.0 lets you sign it.
Discover and verify the remote card
Fetch the garage agent’s card from its well-known path, check the signature against keys you trust, and confirm the skill you need is listed.
Send a message, get a Task
SendMessage starts the work and returns a Task with an id and a state, usually TASK_STATE_WORKING. The remote agent stays opaque: you see states and results, not its tools.
Follow states; answer questions
Streaming delivers each state change as it happens. INPUT_REQUIRED is an interrupted state: answer it in a new message on the same task and work resumes.
Collect artifacts; map failures
COMPLETED carries the artifacts, here the approved estimate. FAILED, CANCELED or REJECTED are terminal: hand them to your own retry or escalation policy.

import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

ALL_TOOLS = load_mcp_tool_definitions()   # 240 tools from 6 MCP servers    #@1
KEEP = {"get_client", "get_holdings", "create_ticket", "send_message"}      #@2

tools = [{"type": "tool_search_tool_bm25_20251119",                        #@3
          "name": "tool_search_tool_bm25"}]      # never deferred           #@3
tools += [{**t, "defer_loading": t["name"] not in KEEP}                    #@2
          for t in ALL_TOOLS]                    # all still sent           #@2

r = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5", max_tokens=1024, tools=tools,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
               "Client NS-2210 wants to stop her SIP from next month."}])

for block in r.content:
    if block.type == "server_tool_use":                                    #@4
        print("searched:", block.input)       # e.g. {"query": "stop SIP mandate"}  #@4
    elif block.type == "tool_search_tool_result":                          #@5
        print("found:", [t.tool_name for t in block.content.tool_references])  #@5
    elif block.type == "tool_use":                                         #@6
        print("calls:", block.name, block.input)  # run it like any tool   #@6
steps: Start from the whole library
Six MCP servers bring 240 tools. Loaded together, their definitions take about 43,000 tokens on every call, and past roughly 30 to 50 tools the model starts picking the wrong one.
Keep a few, defer the rest

The four tools used in most tasks stay loaded. Every other tool is marked defer_loading. They are still sent with each request, because the API needs them to search, but the model does not see them yet.
Add a search tool
The BM25 search tool is added once and never deferred. The model now knows it can look for a capability instead of scanning a huge list.
The model searches
Asked to stop a SIP, the model sees no suitable tool among the four, so it searches: “stop SIP mandate”. That search is one extra step, which is why common tools stay loaded.
Matching tools are loaded
The search returns references to up to 5 matching tools. The API expands them into full definitions, so only those few are added to the context.
Call the tool it found
The model calls cancel_sip_mandate with the client and date. Your loop runs it exactly like any other tool; search changed only which tools the model could see.

import base64, hashlib, secrets, time

MCP_URL = "https://mcp.dhandisha.example/mcp"
TOOL_SCOPES = {                                                      #@2
    "get_portfolio":  "portfolio:read",                              #@2
    "get_statements": "statements:read",                             #@2
    "start_sip":      "sip:write",                                   #@2
    "redeem_units":   "redeem:write",                                #@2
    "update_mandate": "mandate:write",                               #@2
}

def pkce_pair():                                                      #@1
    verifier = secrets.token_urlsafe(64)                              #@1
    digest = hashlib.sha256(verifier.encode()).digest()               #@1
    challenge = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(digest).rstrip(b"=").decode()  #@1
    return verifier, challenge                                        #@1

def connect(user_id):
    verifier, challenge = pkce_pair()                                 #@1
    url = authorize_url(code_challenge=challenge, code_challenge_method="S256",  #@1
                        scope="portfolio:read statements:read",       #@3  reads only, for now
                        resource=MCP_URL)                             #@1  token is for this server
    code = wait_for_redirect(user_id, url)        # the user signs in and consents  #@3
    vault.put(user_id, exchange_code(code, verifier))                 #@5

def token_for(user_id, tool):
    tok = vault.get(user_id)                                          #@5
    if tok.expires_at - time.time() < 60:         # 15-minute access tokens  #@4
        tok = refresh(tok.refresh_token)          # silent; rotates the refresh token  #@4
        vault.put(user_id, tok)                                       #@4
    need = TOOL_SCOPES[tool]                                          #@2
    if need not in tok.scopes:                                        #@3
        raise StepUpConsent(user_id, need)        # ask the user; never widen silently  #@3
    return downscope(tok, need)                   # a token for this one tool  #@2

def call_tool(user_id, tool, args):
    token = token_for(user_id, tool)              # the model never sees this  #@5
    result = mcp_call(MCP_URL, tool, args, bearer=token)              #@5
    audit.log(user=user_id, tool=tool, scope=TOOL_SCOPES[tool])       #@6
    return result                                 # only data goes back to the model  #@5

def disconnect(user_id):
    revoke(vault.get(user_id).refresh_token)      # RFC 7009 revocation  #@6
    vault.delete(user_id)                                             #@6
steps: Sign in with OAuth 2.1 and PKCE

connect() sends the user to the authorization server with a PKCE challenge: the SHA-256 of a random verifier. Only the holder of the verifier can swap the returned code for a token, so a code stolen from the redirect is useless. The resource parameter names the MCP server, so the token is valid there and nowhere else.
One scope per tool

Each of Dhan Disha’s five tools maps to one scope. Reading a portfolio needs portfolio:read; redeeming units needs redeem:write. downscope() hands each call a token carrying only its tool’s scope, so a read call cannot redeem.
Consent to reads now, writes when needed

At sign-up the user grants only the two read scopes. The first time the agent needs to redeem or change a mandate, token_for() raises StepUpConsent and the user sees exactly what is being added. The token is never widened silently.
Short-lived tokens, silent refresh

Access tokens last 15 minutes. When one is about to expire, the refresh token gets a new one without asking the user, and the refresh token itself is rotated. A leaked access token works for minutes, not days, and the user sees no extra prompts.
Keep secrets in the vault, not the prompt

Tokens live in an encrypted vault keyed by user. call_tool() fetches the token and attaches it to the HTTP call; the model only receives the tool’s result. A prompt injection can steer a call, but it cannot make the model reveal a secret it never saw.
Log every call, revoke on disconnect

Each call is logged with the user, tool and scope, so an auditor can see who each action was for. When a user disconnects, the refresh token is revoked at the authorization server and deleted from the vault, and access ends within 15 minutes.

steps: Name and describe it precisely
The name and description are all the agent sees up front. “Respond to a card chargeback … Use when a customer disputes a card transaction” tells it exactly when to load this skill.
Load the body only when needed
Thirty descriptions cost about 3,000 tokens. The full instructions of this skill load only for chargeback tasks.
Script the exact parts
Deadlines depend on the card network and dates. A script computes them; the model never does date arithmetic in its head.
Point to reference files
Evidence rules per reason code live in a separate file, read only when the task gets that far.
Put limits in the skill
Amounts above ₹25,000 go to a person. The skill carries the policy, not just the steps.
Review and version skills
Skills change the agent’s behaviour, so they go through review like code. A downloaded skill is read before it is installed.

code:
import json, anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

tools = [{
    "name": "get_transaction_status",
    "description": ("Look up the status of a UPI payment by its 12-digit UTR number. "
                    "Use it whenever the user asks whether a payment succeeded, failed or was reversed. "
                    "Never guess a status; if the user has not given a UTR, ask for it. "
                    "Returns status, amount in INR and the time of the last update."),
    "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                     "properties": {"utr": {"type": "string", "description": "12-digit UTR"}},
                     "required": ["utr"], "additionalProperties": False},
    "strict": True,                                   # inputs always match the schema
}]

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Did UTR 412345678901 go through?"}]
for step in range(6):                                 # step cap
    resp = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
                                  tools=tools, tool_choice={"type": "auto"}, messages=messages)
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        print(next(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text")); break
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
    results = []
    for b in resp.content:
        if b.type != "tool_use":
            continue
        try:
            out = get_transaction_status(**b.input)
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b.id, "content": json.dumps(out)})
        except Exception as e:                        # send the failure back, don't drop it
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b.id,
                            "content": f"Lookup failed: {e}", "is_error": True})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

from datetime import date
from typing import Annotated, Literal
from fastmcp import FastMCP
from fastmcp.exceptions import ToolError

mcp = FastMCP("opd-scheduling")

@mcp.tool
def find_doctor_availability(
    department: Literal["cardiology", "orthopaedics", "paediatrics", "general_medicine"],
    on_date: Annotated[date, "Clinic date in ISO 8601, e.g. 2026-10-03"],
    response_format: Literal["concise", "detailed"] = "concise",
) -> list[dict]:
    """Find doctors with free OPD slots in one department on one date.
    Use this before book_opd_slot: it already combines the roster, leave and booked slots.
    Do not use it for a patient's existing appointments (use get_patient_appointments).
    Returns at most 10 doctors; 'concise' gives doctor_id, name and free slot times only."""
    today = date.today()
    if on_date < today:
        raise ToolError(f"on_date must be today ({today.isoformat()}) or later; "
                        f"you sent {on_date.isoformat()}. Check the year and try again.")
    rows = roster.free_slots(department, on_date)[:10]
    if response_format == "concise":
        return [{"doctor_id": r.id, "name": r.name, "free": r.slots} for r in rows]
    return [r.model_dump() for r in rows]

code:
import asyncio, json

READS = {"search_fares", "hotel_availability"}          # independent, no side effects

async def run_one(block, timeout=5.0):
    try:
        out = await asyncio.wait_for(TOOLS[block.name](**block.input), timeout)
        return {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": json.dumps(out)}
    except Exception as e:                               # a failure never drops its siblings
        return {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                "content": f"Error: {e!r}", "is_error": True}

async def run_turn(resp):
    calls = [b for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    reads = [c for c in calls if c.name in READS]
    others = [c for c in calls if c.name not in READS]
    results = list(await asyncio.gather(*(run_one(c) for c in reads)))
    for c in others:                                     # dependent or side-effecting: in order
        results.append(await run_one(c))
    order = {c.id: i for i, c in enumerate(calls)}
    results.sort(key=lambda r: order[r["tool_use_id"]])
    return {"role": "user", "content": results}          # all results in one message
parallel.note: TOOLS maps tool names to your async functions. Results are returned in the order the model asked for them.

import time, uuid, httpx

BASE = "https://agents.example-garage.in"
card = httpx.get(f"{BASE}/.well-known/agent-card.json").json()
verify_card_signature(card)                           # reject unsigned or unverifiable cards
assert any(s["id"] == "negotiate_estimate" for s in card["skills"])
A2A_URL = f"{BASE}/a2a"                               # the JSON-RPC endpoint the card lists

def rpc(method: str, params: dict) -> dict:
    r = httpx.post(A2A_URL, timeout=30, headers={"A2A-Version": "1.0", "Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"},
                   json={"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": str(uuid.uuid4()), "method": method, "params": params})
    r.raise_for_status()
    body = r.json()
    if "error" in body:
        raise RuntimeError(body["error"])
    return body["result"]

def msg(text: str, **ids) -> dict:
    return {"message": {"messageId": str(uuid.uuid4()), "role": "ROLE_USER", "parts": [{"text": text}], **ids}}

res = rpc("SendMessage", msg("Agree a repair estimate for claim CLM-88412 within ₹62,000."))
task = res.get("task", res)
DONE = {"TASK_STATE_COMPLETED", "TASK_STATE_FAILED", "TASK_STATE_CANCELED", "TASK_STATE_REJECTED"}
while task["status"]["state"] not in DONE:
    if task["status"]["state"] == "TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED":   # interrupted, not failed
        question = task["status"]["message"]["parts"][0]["text"]
        res = rpc("SendMessage", msg(ask_claims_handler(question),
                                     taskId=task["id"], contextId=task["contextId"]))
        task = res.get("task", res)
    else:
        time.sleep(5)
        task = rpc("GetTask", {"id": task["id"]})
estimate = task.get("artifacts", [])

import numpy as np

TOOLS = load_mcp_tool_definitions()          # 240 definitions
vecs = embed([t["name"] + ": " + t["description"] for t in TOOLS])

find_tools = {
    "name": "find_tools",
    "description": ("Search the tool library by what you need to do, in plain words. "
                    "Use it when none of the loaded tools fits. Returns matching tools."),
    "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                     "properties": {"need": {"type": "string"}},
                     "required": ["need"]}}

def run_find_tools(need: str, k: int = 5):
    scores = vecs @ embed([need])[0]           # cosine if vectors are normalised
    best = np.argsort(-scores)[:k]
    return [{"type": "tool_reference", "tool_name": TOOLS[i]["name"]} for i in best]

KEEP = {"get_client", "get_holdings", "create_ticket", "send_message"}
tools = [find_tools] + [{**t, "defer_loading": t["name"] not in KEEP} for t in TOOLS]

# In your tool loop, answer a find_tools call with:
# {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": call.id,
#  "content": run_find_tools(**call.input)}

toolauth.sc: Dhan Disha, a fictional wealth app, lets 50,000 investors connect their accounts to its assistant, which reaches the app’s MCP server through five tools: portfolio, statements, SIPs, redemptions and bank mandates. code:
from pydantic import AnyUrl
from mcp import ClientSession
from mcp.client.auth import OAuthClientProvider, TokenStorage
from mcp.client.streamable_http import streamablehttp_client
from mcp.shared.auth import OAuthClientInformationFull, OAuthClientMetadata, OAuthToken

MCP_URL = "https://mcp.dhandisha.example/mcp"


class VaultTokenStorage(TokenStorage):
    """One entry per user in the secret store. The model never sees these values."""

    def __init__(self, user_id: str):
        self.path = f"dhan-disha/{user_id}/mcp"

    async def get_tokens(self) -> OAuthToken | None:
        raw = await vault.read(self.path + "/tokens")
        return OAuthToken.model_validate_json(raw) if raw else None

    async def set_tokens(self, tokens: OAuthToken) -> None:
        await vault.write(self.path + "/tokens", tokens.model_dump_json())

    async def get_client_info(self) -> OAuthClientInformationFull | None:
        raw = await vault.read(self.path + "/client")
        return OAuthClientInformationFull.model_validate_json(raw) if raw else None

    async def set_client_info(self, info: OAuthClientInformationFull) -> None:
        await vault.write(self.path + "/client", info.model_dump_json())


def auth_for(user_id: str) -> OAuthClientProvider:
    async def on_redirect(url: str) -> None:        # show this user the consent screen
        await send_consent_link(user_id, url)

    async def on_callback() -> tuple[str, str | None]:
        return await wait_for_code(user_id)        # (code, state) from your redirect URI

    return OAuthClientProvider(
        server_url=MCP_URL,
        client_metadata=OAuthClientMetadata(
            client_name="Dhan Disha assistant",
            redirect_uris=[AnyUrl("https://app.dhandisha.example/oauth/callback")],
            grant_types=["authorization_code", "refresh_token"],
            response_types=["code"],
            scope="portfolio:read statements:read",  # write scopes are requested later
        ),
        storage=VaultTokenStorage(user_id),
        redirect_handler=on_redirect,
        callback_handler=on_callback,
    )


async def get_portfolio(user_id: str):
    async with streamablehttp_client(MCP_URL, auth=auth_for(user_id)) as (read, write, _):
        async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
            await session.initialize()
            result = await session.call_tool("get_portfolio", {})
    audit_log(user=user_id, tool="get_portfolio", scope="portfolio:read")
    return result.content                        # only data goes back to the model
toolauth.note: vault, send_consent_link and wait_for_code stand for your secret store and web app. Class and function names follow the MCP Python SDK at the time of writing (streamablehttp_client may be named streamable_http_client in newer releases, and stateless protocol revisions may not need initialize()); check the SDK version you install.

fcall.title: Returning parallel tool results
fcall.code:
results = []
for block in resp.content:
    if block.type == "tool_use":
        out = run_tool(block.name, block.input)
        results.append({"type": "tool_result",
                        "tool_use_id": resp.content[0].id,
                        "content": json.dumps(out)})
messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
fcall.explain: Every result is labelled with the id of the first content block, which may not even be a tool call. Each tool_result must carry the id of the call it answers; otherwise results are misattributed or the API rejects the request because some tool_use ids have no result.

also.3: Filtering for tool_use blocks is right; text blocks need no result.
also.8: Putting all results in one user message is correct: that is how parallel results must be returned.

tooldesign.title: A tool error the model can use
tooldesign.explain: An opaque code tells the model something failed but not what or how to fix it, so it retries blindly or gives up. It is also returned as an ordinary result rather than an error. Raise an error that names the problem, the value received and the fix, so the model can correct the date in one retry.
tooldesign.fix: raise ToolError(f"on_date must be today ({date.today()}) or later; you sent {on_date}.")

also.2: Dept is an enum of valid departments, which is good parameter design.
also.7: Returning a concise projection of at most 10 rows is good result design.

parallel.title: Which calls can run together?
parallel.explain: The charge depends on the order: it should carry the order id, and it must not run if creating the order fails. Running both at once can charge a card for an order that was never created. Side-effecting calls that depend on each other run in order.
parallel.fix:
order = await create_order(cart)
    receipt = await charge_card(card, price.total, order_id=order.id)

also.2: Price and stock are independent reads, so gathering them is correct.
also.3: Checking stock before any write is the right order.

idempotency.title: Retrying a refund
idempotency.explain: A new key on every attempt makes each retry look like a new refund, so a timeout after the refund ran causes a second refund. The key must be created once per logical action and reused on every attempt.
idempotency.fix: key = f"refund-{dispute_id}"          # the same key on every attempt

also.6: Retrying only on timeouts is reasonable for this call.
also.7: This is full jitter: a random wait between 0 and 0.5 × 2^attempt seconds.

mcp.title: Validating an access token
mcp.code:
def authorize(request):
    token = request.headers["Authorization"].removeprefix("Bearer ")
    claims = jwt.decode(token, signing_key, algorithms=["RS256"], issuer=ISSUER,
                        options={"verify_aud": False})
    if "folio:read" not in claims["scope"].split():
        raise Forbidden("insufficient_scope", scope="folio:read")
    return claims
mcp.explain: With the audience check off, any valid token from the company’s identity provider is accepted, including one issued for a different application. MCP servers must validate that tokens were issued for them, and must never pass the client’s token through to downstream APIs.

also.3: Pinning the algorithm and the issuer is correct.
also.5: Checking scopes and answering insufficient_scope is correct.

a2a.title: Polling an A2A task
a2a.explain: INPUT_REQUIRED is an interrupted state, not a terminal one: the remote agent is waiting for an answer. Treating it as done makes the client stop and mark a healthy task as failed. Handle it by sending the answer on the same task.

also.4: Polling GetTask is valid when streaming or push is not available.
also.8: Only COMPLETED counts as success; the other terminal states do not.

toolsearch.title: Deferring the search tool too
toolsearch.code:
tools = [{"type": "tool_search_tool_bm25_20251119", "name": "tool_search_tool_bm25"}]
tools += ALL_TOOLS
for t in tools:
    t["defer_loading"] = True
r = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024,
                           tools=tools, messages=messages)
toolsearch.fix: t["defer_loading"] = t["name"] not in KEEP   # KEEP holds the search tool and common tools
toolsearch.explain: Every tool is deferred, including the search tool itself, so the model can see nothing and the request fails. The search tool must never be deferred, and the few most-used tools should stay loaded so common tasks skip the search.

also.1: Correct: the BM25 search tool is added once.
also.5: Correct: all definitions are still sent; only what the model sees changes.

toolauth.title: A token in the system prompt
toolauth.fix: system = "You are Dhan Disha's assistant. Tools are already authorised for this user."
toolauth.explain: The access token is written into the system prompt, so the model can repeat it: a prompt injection in a statement or email can ask it to print the header, and the prompt is also stored in traces. A copied token works outside the agent. The tool layer already attaches the token in call_tool, so the prompt never needs it.

also.2: Correct: the token comes from the vault, keyed by user.
also.8: Correct: the tool layer fetches a token scoped to this tool and attaches it in code.

skills.code:

The function name’s length

At 400 ms

fcall: A UPI app’s assistant is asked “Did UTR 412345678901 go through?” It has a get_transaction_status tool. What does the model actually return when it decides to use the tool?
The payment status, fetched from the switch
A tool_use block with an id, the tool name and the UTR as an argument
A Python function call that the API runs on your server
A request for your database credentials
The model never runs tools. It returns a structured call; your code executes it and returns the result.
Your code runs a balance lookup and sends back the result. What must the tool_result block contain so the model can use it?
The tool_use_id of the call it answers
Each result is matched to its call by id; without the right tool_use_id the result cannot be attributed.
A recharge assistant greets a user who says “Thanks, bye!”. The request uses tool_choice any on every turn. What happens?
The model is forced to call a tool on every turn and cannot reply in text
The API ignores tool_choice for greetings
The model calls every tool once and then answers
any requires a tool call in each response, so a loop that always sends it never lets the model answer in text.
A PNR-status question needs one lookup. With tool_choice auto, how many model turns does the exchange take, including the answer?
Turn 1 returns the call; after your code sends the result, turn 2 is the answer.
A claims assistant’s model sometimes sends policy_no as a number instead of the string the schema requires. What is the most direct fix?
Turn on strict schemas so sampling is constrained to the schema
Add “please use strings” to the system prompt
Strict mode uses grammar-constrained sampling so inputs always match the schema.
An order-tracking tool throws a timeout. What should your loop send back?
A tool_result for that call with is_error true and a short message
A new user message asking the model to try again
Every call needs a result; an error result lets the model retry, try another path or explain.
A brokerage assistant defines get_holdings. Which belong in a good tool definition? Select all that apply.
A name that says what it does
A description of when to use it and when not
A JSON Schema for the inputs
The user’s password for the trading API
Name, description and input schema define a tool. Credentials stay in your executor, never in the definition.
A lab-report assistant has a step whose only job is to extract fields into a record_vitals call. When is forcing that tool reasonable?
On every turn of every conversation
For that one extraction step, typically on the first request only
Only when the model is uncertain
Forcing a specific tool suits a step that must produce a structured call; afterwards switch back to auto.

A question needs 3 dependent lookups. Each turn resends 2,000 tokens of prompt and tool definitions, and each tool result adds 300 tokens that stay in the history. Ignoring model output, how many input tokens does the exchange use?
An OpenAI-based assistant returns function results. Which field ties a function output to the call it answers?
OpenAI matches outputs to calls by call_id, as Anthropic does with tool_use_id.
A loan assistant’s loop sometimes never ends. Which safeguards help? Select all that apply.
A step cap on model turns
Stopping forcing a tool after the first request
Returning errors as is_error so the model can conclude
A cap bounds the loop, forcing only once lets the model answer, and error results let it wrap up. Removing descriptions makes things worse.
With tool_choice none, a student asks “What is my exam hall number?” and a lookup tool exists. What happens?
The model calls the tool anyway
The model answers without calling any tool, so it cannot know the hall
The tool is called automatically by the API
none prevents tool calls, so a question that needs data gets an answer without it.
An engineer sets tool_choice {"type":"tool","name":"refund"} and gets HTTP 400 on one current model with extended thinking enabled. What is the likely cause?
The refund tool has too long a description
Forcing a specific tool is not supported in that configuration, so fall back to auto
The API key lacks refund permission
Forced tool_choice (any or tool) is not supported with extended thinking and is rejected by some current models.
Which statements about the tool loop are true? Select all that apply.
The model decides whether to call a tool when tool_choice is auto
A response can contain more than one tool_use block
The model can read your database directly once a tool is defined
The model chooses, your code executes, and several calls can appear in one response. The model never gets direct access.
A policy tool’s schema uses a JSON Schema feature that strict mode does not support. What should you expect?
Strict mode silently ignores the feature and still guarantees validity
The request can be rejected; strict supports a subset of JSON Schema, so simplify the schema
The model ignores the whole schema
The tool is called without arguments
Strict mode supports only a subset of JSON Schema, so unsupported features must be removed or rewritten.
An agent runs 5,000 conversations a day. 40% need one lookup, 30% two sequential lookups and 30% none. With tool_choice auto, how many tool calls a day?
OpenAI’s guidance on how many functions to make available at the start of a turn is roughly what?
OpenAI suggests keeping fewer than 20 functions available at the start of a turn for accuracy.
A clinic assistant’s calls sometimes fail validation. Which fixes address the arguments themselves? Select all that apply.
Use enums and clear parameter descriptions
Switch the loop to streaming output
Strict mode and clearer, constrained parameters improve argument validity; token limits and streaming do not.
Which benchmark is designed to score how accurately models form function calls, including parallel and multi-turn calls?
BFCL, the Berkeley function-calling benchmark, evaluates simple, multiple, parallel and multi-turn function calling.
Which situations are better served by calling an API directly from your code, without letting a model choose tools? Select all that apply.
A nightly job that always fetches the same shipment report
A fixed webhook that always posts a delivery status to one endpoint
A chat assistant answering open questions about orders
An agent that must decide which of several lookups a question needs
Fixed pipelines need no model decision. Open questions and choosing between lookups are where tool calling helps.
tooldesign: A support agent has search_txn, find_transaction and lookup_payment, and uses them interchangeably with poor results. What is the best first fix?
Add a fourth search tool for edge cases
Merge them into one search_transactions tool with clear filters and a full description
Remove all descriptions to save tokens
Force the model to call all three every time
Overlapping tools split the model’s choices; one task-shaped tool with a clear description removes the ambiguity.
According to Anthropic’s guidance, what is by far the most important factor in tool performance?
The length of the tool name
The output format of the model
Anthropic calls detailed descriptions by far the most important factor, aiming for 3–4 sentences or more.
A calendar agent must list users, list events and then create an event to book a meeting. What does good tool design suggest?
One schedule_event tool that finds availability and books
Add a fourth tool that calls the other three
Consolidate chains of thin calls into one task-shaped tool that does what the user asked.
A tool returns full 4,100-token product records when the next step needs only id, price and stock. With concise results of 380 tokens, and 3 calls per task, how many result tokens are saved per task?
A booking tool returns {"error": "E422"} when the date is in the past. What happens next, typically?
The model corrects the date immediately
The model retries blindly or gives up, because the code gives no hint
Opaque codes give the model nothing to act on; actionable errors let it correct itself in one retry.
Which make a parameter unambiguous? Select all that apply.
Naming it customer_id rather than user
Giving an example format for dates
Specific names, enums and examples remove ambiguity; a generic name such as data does the opposite.
An agent loads 60 tools on every turn and accuracy has dropped. What does Anthropic suggest past roughly 30–50 tools?
Load tool definitions on demand with tool search
Shorten every description to one word
Selection accuracy degrades with many tools; tool search loads only relevant definitions.
40 tools of 350 definition tokens each are sent on each of 6 turns. With tool search, each turn carries a 500-token search tool plus 5 loaded tools. How many definition tokens are saved per task?
You connect tools from several services to one agent. Which help the model tell them apart? Select all that apply.
Descriptions that say when not to use a tool
Namespaces and explicit “when not to use” guidance separate similar tools; identical names or missing schemas add confusion.
Which error message best helps the model self-correct?
“pickup_date must be today or later; you sent 2025-10-03. Check the year.”
It names the rule, the value received and the fix.
Claude Code caps tool responses by default at about how many tokens?
Anthropic’s engineering post notes Claude Code restricts tool responses to 25,000 tokens by default.
An agent’s search tool returns long raw JSON with UUIDs. Which result changes help? Select all that apply.
Return human-readable names alongside or instead of opaque ids
Return every field so nothing is missed
Semantic fields, pagination and a concise mode make results high-signal. Returning everything floods the context.
How should you confirm a redesign of tool descriptions actually helped?
Ask the model which version it prefers
Run a task set, score tool choice and arguments, and read failing transcripts
Tool design is prompt design: evaluate it on realistic tasks before and after.
A tool definition averages 250 tokens. An agent exposes 32 tools on every turn of a 5-turn task. How many definition tokens per task?
Which are signs of poor tool design in agent transcripts? Select all that apply.
The model calls two tools that do almost the same thing in one task
The model retries the same bad argument several times
The model calls a tool once and answers
The model asks the user for a missing account number
Near-duplicate calls and blind retries point to overlapping tools and unhelpful errors. The other two are good behaviour.
Anthropic’s example cut a Slack-thread result from 206 tokens to 72 with a concise format. Roughly what fraction was removed?
In MCP, how should a tool report that an input failed validation, so the model can self-correct?
As a JSON-RPC protocol error only
As a tool execution error in the result, with isError true
MCP puts input-validation failures in tool execution errors (isError true) so the model can see and fix them.
A hospital replaces 30 thin EHR endpoints with 8 task tools. Which benefits should you expect? Select all that apply.
Task-shaped tools reduce calls, ambiguity and definition tokens, but nothing guarantees zero errors.
Which description is best for a refund tool?
“Refunds a settled UPI payment by UTR, up to the original amount. Use only after the dispute is approved; do not use for failed payments, which auto-reverse. Returns refund id and status.”
“Use this tool for everything related to money.”
It says what, when, when not and what it returns.
Which tools help you design and test tool interfaces? Select all that apply.
MCP Inspector, to call tools by hand and read raw results
promptfoo, to score tool choice across a task set
A CDN, to cache tool definitions
A load balancer, to spread tool calls
Inspector shows exactly what the model sees; promptfoo measures behaviour across tasks. The others are infrastructure.
parallel: A KYC turn asks for PAN (600 ms), CKYC (700 ms), Aadhaar OTP status (900 ms) and bureau (1,200 ms) checks, all independent. Run concurrently, how long do they take?
Concurrent independent calls finish with the slowest one: 1,200 ms.
In the same flow, open_account (400 ms) needs all four checks. What is the wall-clock time for the whole turn?
1,200 ms for the slowest check, then 400 ms: 1,600 ms.
Calls A (300 ms), B (800 ms) and C (500 ms) are independent. D (400 ms) needs B. E (200 ms) needs C and D. What is the wall-clock time?
How should results from three parallel tool calls be returned to Claude?
All three tool_result blocks in one user message, before any text
As plain text in the next user question
All results go in one user message; splitting them discourages later parallel calls.
A batch runs create_order and charge_card(order_id=...) together in one gather. What is wrong?
The charge depends on the order id, so it must run after create_order succeeds
A call that needs another call’s output, especially a write, must wait for it.
A plan-comparison turn fans out four price lookups; one times out. What should the response to the model contain? Select all that apply.
One result with is_error for the timeout
All four tool_result blocks in one message
No results, because the batch failed
Every call gets a result; the failure is marked, not allowed to drop its siblings.
Which Claude setting turns off parallel tool calls?
With tool_choice auto and disable_parallel_tool_use true, how many tool calls can one response contain?
With auto it can make at most one call; with any or tool, exactly one.
Four independent carrier-rate calls take 400, 900, 650 and 1,100 ms. How much time does running them in parallel save over sequential?
Sequential 3,050 ms; parallel 1,100 ms; saved 1,950 ms.
Which calls are safe to put in the same parallel batch? Select all that apply.
Approve the claim, then pay it out
Create a payout that needs the approval id
Independent reads can run together; the approval and the payout that depends on it cannot.
A lab agent makes 6 independent calls of 500 ms each, but a partner API allows only 2 concurrent requests. What is the fastest possible wall-clock time?
Three waves of two calls: 3 × 500 = 1,500 ms.
A research agent adds a fifth independent 700 ms lookup to four others whose slowest takes 1,100 ms. What happens to wall-clock time?
The new call finishes before the slowest existing one, so the critical path is unchanged.
In asyncio, one call in gather raises and you did not catch it. What is the risk?
Nothing; other results are still returned
The exception propagates, and without per-call handling you return no results for the batch
The failed call is retried automatically
Catch errors per call so every call still produces a result.
Which benchmark categories does BFCL cover? Select all that apply.
BFCL scores simple, multiple, parallel and parallel-multiple calls, plus multi-turn tasks from v3.
A dependent chain is 300 → 500 → 200 ms, and two other independent calls take 700 and 900 ms. What is the wall-clock time?
The chain takes 1,000 ms, longer than 900 ms, so it is the critical path.
A travel agent checks three airlines and a hotel at once, then books. Why must the flight and hotel bookings run after the searches?
Each booking needs a fare or room id returned by a search
The model cannot emit two calls
Bookings depend on search output and have side effects, so they wait.
Which statements about parallel tool calls are true? Select all that apply.
The speed-up is bounded by the longest dependent chain
A skipped call should still return a result
Parallel calls always reduce cost per token
Every call in a batch must use the same tool
Critical path bounds the speed-up and every call needs a result. Parallelism does not change token prices, and calls can use different tools.
Five independent calls take 200 ms each. Run sequentially they take 1,000 ms. Run in parallel, what is the speed-up?
A call is skipped because the call it depended on failed. What should its result say?
An error such as “Not executed: the preceding call failed”
The result of the failed call
Anthropic’s guidance returns an is_error result explaining it was not executed.
A dispatcher’s fan-out of 40 lookups triggers 429 errors. Which fixes help? Select all that apply.
Increase the number of concurrent calls to finish sooner
Limiting concurrency and backing off with jitter respect the rate limit; more concurrency makes it worse.
idempotency: A refund call times out at 10 s but the refund had actually gone through. The agent retries without an idempotency key. What happens?
Without a key the gateway cannot tell the retry from a new refund.
Where should the idempotency key for a refund be created?
Inside the retry loop, fresh on each attempt
Once per logical refund, stored and reused on every attempt
By the model in its arguments each time
By the gateway after the first attempt
One action, one key, reused on every retry, even after a restart.
1,000 refunds; 30% of responses are lost after the refund runs, independently per attempt. The client retries up to 2 times with no key. How many duplicate refunds are expected?
Stripe receives a repeat request with the same idempotency key but different parameters. What does it do?
Processes it as a new request
Returns an error, because the parameters differ
Stripe compares parameters and errors if a key is reused with different ones.
Which errors are generally worth retrying automatically?
Transient errors can succeed on retry; other 4xx errors need a change.
AWS’s full jitter formula for the wait before a retry is:
Full jitter picks a random wait between 0 and the capped exponential value.
With base 0.5 s and cap 8 s, what is the maximum full-jitter wait before attempt 4 (using 2^4)?
Which tools need an idempotency key before an agent may retry them? Select all that apply.
Writes that move money or send messages repeat their side effect; a status read is safe to retry.
Each attempt fails 30% of the time independently. With 3 retries (4 attempts), what share of requests eventually succeed?
Stripe keys can be up to how many characters?
Stripe allows idempotency keys of up to 255 characters.
Under the IETF Idempotency-Key draft, what status suits a duplicate request that arrives while the first is still being processed?
The draft recommends 409 Conflict for a concurrent duplicate, and 422 for a reused key with a different payload.
A payout service shows retry storms after brief outages. Which changes help? Select all that apply.
Add full jitter to the backoff
Retry immediately in a tight loop
Jitter spreads retries; caps bound total load. Tight loops make storms worse.
In MCP tool annotations, what is the default value of destructiveHint?
destructiveHint defaults to true and idempotentHint to false, so hosts assume the worst.
Which statements about MCP annotations are true? Select all that apply.
Annotations from untrusted servers should be treated as untrusted
readOnlyHint guarantees the server cannot write
Hints default to the cautious values and are only hints, especially from untrusted servers.
Temporal’s documentation says what about business-logic Activities?
You should always make them idempotent
They run exactly once by design
“You should always make your business logic Activities idempotent,” because they may be retried.
A refund of ₹2,499 is duplicated for 39 out of every 100 customers across 1,000 refunds. How much is overpaid?
An idempotent write, such as setting a data cap to 10 GB, is retried after a timeout. What happens?
The end state is the same: 10 GB
Repeating an idempotent write leaves the same state.
How should a server implement idempotency keys? Select all that apply.
Claim the key atomically, for example with SET NX, before running the action
Store the first response and replay it for repeats with the same key
Generate a new key for each repeat
Delete the key as soon as the first response is sent
Atomic claim plus stored responses make repeats safe; new or deleted keys defeat the purpose.
The client times out while the server is still processing a charge. Which case is the dangerous one for duplicates?
